**International Copper Study Group Statistical Committee Thirty-Fourth Regular Meeting 6**<sup>**th**</sup> **October 2009, 4.00pm-6.00pm Lisbon, Portugal** 

**ICSG/STAT34/2** 

## **Statistical Committee Forecast Comparisons and Accuracy of ICSG Forecast (Agenda Item 2)** 

# **<u>Introduction</u>** 

This report is produced annually by the Secretariat, with the aim of assessing the accuracy of ICSG supply and demand forecasts. 

In its efforts to produce the best possible forecast the Secretariat sources its data through: 

- _ICSG Member Countries_ - provide the Secretariat with a Forecast Survey for their own country; 

- _Industry_ - direct contacts with companies that provide the Secretariat with production plans and their view on the development of their country’s copper industry; 

- _Analysts/Metals Associations_ , that collaborate with the Secretariat in providing data or information related to specific requests and their views on the market. 

- _Government organizations from nonmember countries,_ provide current data and outlooks if available 

For some countries where data is not available or cannot be directly sourced, the Secretariat endeavors to put forward its best estimates.  Estimates are based on elements such as economic indicators, trends in industry development such as closures or start-up of new mines or plants, anecdotal evidence, analyst’s information, etc.  For some countries (eg Congo and Zambia) profiles are made with data on a company by company basis to allow a better assessment of the overall country outlook. 

The degree of accuracy of the projections produced by the Study Group is dependent on numerous factors such as the accuracy of forecasts received from each Study Group member country; the ability of industry to comply with its production plans; the performance of the economy vis a vis expectations; the accuracy of the Secretariat estimates; readiness of planned project startups or expansions; previously unannounced plant closures, postponement of planned projects, copper price behavior; and unforeseen factors such as labor issues, technical failures, energy blackouts, shortages of supplies, political instability, accidents or weather conditions. It is worth noting that the past few years have been particularly fertile for the above factors and that the disruption rate has significantly exceeded historical averages. 

One should also bear in mind that the copper industry is one of the most complex industries, bigger in production and usage than most of the other non-ferrous metals markets.  Copper is produced (mined and refined) and used (refined copper usage level) in more than 70 countries, and traded in many more. Because of its size and regional diversity the task of forecasting becomes a complex and difficult exercise. The growth in supply for the next few years is expected to come from countries of less political stability, less skilled labor availability, less infrastructural development or located in

remote places, which increases the probability of delays in the development of the projects currently considered in ICSG forecast. 

As the primary source for data are the forecast surveys received from member countries, member countries are therefore requested to take note of the trends shown in this report and, where differences 

1 

have been identified, to use the relevant information to try to improve future results. This applies in particular to cases where the same error of over or underestimation for a member country has been frequently repeated. 

Rather than using any forecasting model or empirical methodology for its forecasts the ICSG relies on a bottom up approach to develop individual country data elements. 

The compiled projections are then globally adjusted to correct for primary feed shortage and allowances for production disruptions.  The primary feed shortage adjustment takes into consideration the availability of copper concentrates and cross checks it with the primary refined production plans put forward by producers.  If there is a shortage of concentrates the adjustment will reduce the figure for refined production, as the unavailability of raw material will constrain production.  Based on an historical average indexed to capacity utilization and projected capacity growth, the adjustment for production disruptions estimates a quantity for unexpected production disruptions that may occur such as strikes, accidents, operational failures, etc. 

Because of increasing production disruptions and delays in bringing on stream new capacity, the deviation between ICSG productions forecasts and the realized production levels has been rising. Therefore, the Secretariat proposed at the April 2008 meeting changing the calculation for the Disruption Allowance to a moving average of the preceding three years deviation. Previous calculations were based on projected capacity growth and did not accurately reflect market developments. 

In this report, forecasts of production and usage for 2008 presented at previous meetings are compared with actual data for 2008 as currently held in the Study Group’s records (preliminary and still subject to possible revision at the October meeting). The main features of the degree of accuracy achieved in the forecasts for 2008 are summarized.  Trends in the accuracy of the forecasts are also shown for the period 2000-2008.  For this purpose, actual data is compared with the first forecast prepared two years prior to the year concerned and the forecast prepared at the Study Group’s spring meeting of the year concerned. 

Diagrams illustrating the extent of the deviation of the forecasts of total production and usage compared with actual results are also included. 

# **<u>Comparisons for 2008 data</u>** 

2008 was a volatile year for the copper industry as the production side was affected by a number of unforeseen factors such as strikes and labour unrest, accidents and operational failures, lower than an

ticipated ore grades, difficulties with start up of new projects, etc. This kind of situation also occurred in 2006 and 2007 and seems to have become characteristic of a rapidly expanding industry. Such unforeseen factors have widened the deviation between ICSG preliminary productions forecasts and the actual production levels. In 2006 and 2007 the annual deviation between the first forecast for mine production and the actual data was around 850Kt, compared to an average annual deviation of 200Kt in the period 2000-2005. The 2008 deviation proved to be even higher. With the aim of avoiding such wide deviations, beginning with the April 2008 meeting, the Secretariat changed its calculation for the Disruption Allowance to a moving average of the preceding three years deviation. Previous calculations were based on projected capacity growth and did not accurately reflect recent market developments. 2 Beside the combination of such unforeseen factors referred to above, 2008 was further impacted by the fall in copper prices in the second half of 2008 and the deterioration of the world economy that led to a rapid decline in copper usage levels, as well as to mine closures and a reduction in planned production. The global economic recession, which has had a dramatic impact on first half 2009 production and usage, is expected to influence the market well into the coming years and further challenge the ability to project accurate market balances. With mine production forecasts, the deviations to final data are more significant (over estimation of 11.5% in the first forecast and 6.1% in the April 2008 forecast. The major causes for the high deviation in 2008 mine production forecast as compared to actual 2008 data (overestimation) were the strike at Grupo Mexico’s Cananea mine that started in July 2007 and continued throughout 2008; lower than anticipated ore grades at Chilean mines; technical failures at Escondia and Collahuasi (SAG mills); operational issues limiting the access to high grade ore zones at Grasberg and Batu Hijau mines in Indonesia; and over-optimism on bringing new projects on stream owing to start-up problems/and or construction delays, especially in Africa. The Secretariat significantly understated Chinese refined production levels for 2008 (several smelters/refinery expansions occurred) and was too optimistic for Australian and African output. Events in Indonesia and Mexico strongly affected ICSG forecast deviation for 2008 (Indonesia and Mexico represented 31% of the total mine production deviation of the countries included in table 2). At the global level, and including the disruption adjustments, word refined production was overestimated by 781kt in the first forecast made in September 2006 and was over estimated by 332Kt in the April 2008 forecast. If adjustments were not taken into consideration, the overestimation in the first forecast would have been much higher at 1.6Mt. Regarding world copper refined usage, 2008 actual data is 530kt below our expectations at the September 2006 meeting and 486kt below our April 2008 forecast. Deviations in the usage forecast occurred in several countries but the major ones occurred for the United States and China (table 3). In the United States, a severe economical downturn affecting copper usage sectors reduced substantially the actual usage levels (over estimation of 448Kt, 23%) and in China the high level of refined copper imports led to higher than expected apparent usage levels (underestimation of 758Kt, -15%). It is worth reiterating that ICSG calculates Chinese copper usage based on an apparent calculation, not taking into account changes in unreported stocks. The global economic crisis and its negative impact on copper using sectors such as construction and automobile led to a decrease in actual copper usage in the 4th quarter of 2008 in many countries, contributing significantly to the forecast deviations in those countries (e.g.: Japan, the EU, South 4 Korea). Over optimism regarding the development of the semis industry in the Gulf region and unanticipated closures of some plants in France and Canada, also contributed to the forecast deviation. Detailed reasons for the main deviations between country actual usage data and the first country usage forecasts undertaken in September 2006 are listed in Table 3 below. recasts the ICSG relies on a bottom up approach to develop individual country data elements. 

- The ICSG forecast for 2008 world refined usage deviated from actual data by 2.9% in the first forecast and by 2.7% in the April 2008 forecast.  Refined production forecast (including adjustments for feed shortage and supply disruptions) deviated by respectively 4.3% and 1.8% in the first and the April 2008 forecasts.  For the mine production forecast, the deviations were much higher when compared to actual data (over estimation of 11.5% in the first forecast and 6.1% in the April 2008 forecast).  These higher differentials in the 2008 forecast were mainly due to a number of unexpected operational and labor problems that occurred in 2008 as well as the impact of the global economical downturn. 

- Predicted surpluses for 2008 ranged from 85kt to 489kt through the various forecasts, actual surplus ended in the middle of the forecast range at 238Kt. Some of the same factors affected both supply and demand leading to offsetting declines in both supply and use 

- When taking the full period 2000-2008, average deviation of the “first forecasts” undertaken for each year is about 3% for mine production, 2.7% for refined production (adjusted) and 3.1% for refined usage.  Average deviation of the spring forecasts undertaken for each year is about 2.6% for mine production, 1.8% for refined production and 2.1% for refined usage. 

9 

- Analyzing the forecast trends, production data seems to be more often overstated as compared to actual data.  In periods of significant developments in new mine or refined capacity, as has been the case for China, India, Africa and Chile for instance, bringing on stream new capacity seems to have taken longer than expected. 

- Over-optimism has also been the trend for the refined usage forecast, most of the time overstated, with the exception of usage in China, were it was normally underestimated. 

- The use of “adjustments” in the forecast (allowances for feed shortage and disruptions) has proved to be an important tool.
